title: Gigaplex
subtitle: A complete game console in a 15 × 11 matrix
summary: I built a CR2032-powered keychain console around a charlieplexed display, five buttons, motion input and sound.
thumbnailAlt: Gigaplex keychain console held between fingers, with part of its LED matrix glowing cyan

content.body: I reduced the interface to hardware that remains understandable at very low resolution: 165 LEDs, directional controls, one confirmation button and physical motion. The result is small enough to live on a keychain without turning every game into the same blinking square.

The design started with a severe interface budget: a 15 × 11 display, five buttons, a buzzer and motion sensing, all in roughly 35 mm square and powered from a coin cell. Every menu and game mechanic therefore had to earn its pixels and its current draw.

The matrix is charlieplexed rather than driven by a large display IC. That saves board area, but it moves complexity into scanning, brightness control and pin-state safety. Each illuminated LED needs one driven pair while the other matrix lines stay high impedance; an incorrect pin state can create a ghost path through LEDs that were meant to be off.

content.alt: Gigaplex hanging beside keys in an open hand, with a band of LEDs illuminated
content.caption: The keyring photograph puts the board and controls at their intended everyday scale.

items.title: Fix the physical pixel budget
items.body: I committed to the 15 × 11 matrix and 2 mm LED pitch first, then designed icons and game screens at that exact resolution instead of shrinking desktop artwork afterwards.

items.title: Allocate the charlieplex network
items.body: Fourteen matrix lines were arranged to address the LEDs while leaving enough MCU pins for five independent buttons, the buzzer, IMU and light sensing.

items.title: Choose interactions that survive low resolution
items.body: Directional buttons handle exact input, while tilt, shake and rotation give the IMU a reason to exist in games such as the sand simulation and dice mode.

items.title: Plan deterministic firmware
items.body: Display scanning, button polling, game updates and buzzer timing were separated so a slow game routine cannot leave the matrix flickering or a note stuck on.

items.title: Assemble and light the first board
items.body: I assembled the populated board with its five switches, keyring opening and rear battery holder. A lit section of the matrix gives me a real electrical bring-up point to inspect.

items.title: Finish the console and packaging
items.body: I finished the console after the first board bring-up and completed its packaging around the keychain-sized hardware.

items.title: Move into mid-scale production
items.body: I am moving the finished design toward mid-scale production, where repeatable assembly, inspection and packaging are the next practical constraints.

content.alt: Assembled Gigaplex console held upright with cyan LEDs lit along the lower part of the matrix
content.caption: First light on the assembled face makes LED spacing and visibility concrete.

content.body: The firmware architecture separates matrix scanning, input polling, game state and buzzer timing so the tiny MCU can keep the display stable while games and IMU-driven effects run.

I kept the physical layout within the same tight budget as the code. The five switches sit directly below the LED field, while the keyring hole shares a corner of the board. On the back, the coin-cell holder occupies most of the available area; the translucent blue case follows that outline without hiding the battery access.

The menu was harder than the games. At this resolution two icons that look distinct on a monitor can merge after the real LED pitch, diffusion and viewing distance are considered, so I repeatedly simplified silhouettes and increased empty space.

Memory is another design constraint rather than a late optimisation. Frame data, games and audio must share a small MCU, which is why the video experiments use compact row and delta commands and a deterministic integer-only decoder.

I could not treat the coin cell like a bench supply. I designed the scan pattern and brightness levels around short, controlled LED drive intervals so the display remains stable alongside the buzzer and IMU without asking the CR2032 for a continuous full-frame load.

content.title: Completed build
content.body: I finished Gigaplex and its packaging. I am now moving the completed design toward mid-scale production.

I used the oscilloscope to inspect the short drive pulses behind the display scan during bring-up. The trace records that electrical work; the photographs show the finished front, controls, battery side and case together as a keychain console.

I wanted the console to feel deliberately tiny rather than compromised. With the product and packaging finished, the next challenge is repeating the build: placing 165 LEDs consistently, checking the assembled matrix and controls, and fitting the case without hand-tuning each unit.
